title: Why does a Hibernate UPDATE set every column even when only one changed? How does dirty checking work, how does @DynamicUpdate fix it, and how can merge() accidentally overwrite columns with null?
shortTitle: Why does Hibernate UPDATE set every column?
topicTitle: Performance — Large IN, Dirty Checking, OSIV

s1_definition.profdef: By default Hibernate caches one static UPDATE statement per entity that sets **every** mapped column, so even if you change a single field, the generated SQL lists all columns. This is a performance optimization — the statement can be prepared once and reused — made possible by **dirty checking**, where Hibernate compares the managed entity to its loaded snapshot to decide *whether* to update, then writes all columns. Adding `@DynamicUpdate` makes Hibernate generate a tailored UPDATE at runtime containing only the changed columns. Separately, `merge()` can accidentally overwrite columns with null if you merge a partially-populated detached entity whose unset fields are null, because merge copies the entire detached state over the managed state.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the bank's update form always has every field printed on it, and the clerk re-writes the customer's entire record — name, address, phone, balance — every time even if only the phone number changed. It is faster to use one pre-printed form than to custom-print a new form each time. But if a customer hands in a form where they only filled the phone number and left name and address blank, and the clerk copies the whole form over the record, the blanks wipe out the existing name and address. That blank-overwrite is the merge null-overwrite trap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Default UPDATE sets all columns (one reusable statement); @DynamicUpdate updates only changed columns; merge() copies the whole detached entity, so null fields can blank existing data.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** By default Hibernate caches one static UPDATE statement per entity that sets **every** mapped column, so even if you change a single field, the generated SQL lists all columns. This is a performance optimization — the statement can be prepared once and reused — made possible by **dirty checking**, where Hibernate compares the managed entity to its loaded snapshot to decide *whether* to update, then writes all columns. Adding `@DynamicUpdate` makes Hibernate generate a tailored UPDATE at runtime containing only the changed columns. Separately, `merge()` can accidentally overwrite columns with null if you merge a partially-populated detached entity whose unset fields are null, because merge copies the entire detached state over the managed state.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the bank's update form always has every field printed on it, and the clerk re-writes the customer's entire record — name, address, phone, balance — every time even if only the phone number changed. It is faster to use one pre-printed form than to custom-print a new form each time. But if a customer hands in a form where they only filled the phone number and left name and address blank, and the clerk copies the whole form over the record, the blanks wipe out the existing name and address. That blank-overwrite is the merge null-overwrite trap.

**One line to remember:** Default UPDATE sets all columns (one reusable statement); @DynamicUpdate updates only changed columns; merge() copies the whole detached entity, so null fields can blank existing data.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a phone-number update triggered an unwanted audit on the balance column.** At National Bank of India, the accounts table had a trigger that logged any change to balance. Because the default UPDATE always wrote balance, even a phone change fired the audit. Adding `@DynamicUpdate` so only the changed column is written stopped the false audit. This is exactly what dynamic update fixes.

**Problem 2 — a profile-update API wiped customers' names.** A developer built an Account from the request body, which only contained the phone, and called merge. Merge copied the null name over the stored name, blanking it. This is exactly the merge null-overwrite trap.

What the code will do: an `AccountUpdateService` with a broken merge-based method (shown and explained) and the correct load-and-mutate partial update with `@DynamicUpdate` on the entity.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: update SAV2001's phone to 9876543210. Stored name is "Rajesh Kumar", balance 1000000.

Step 1 (correct path) — `em.find` loads the full managed Account with name, balance, and phone populated, and Hibernate snapshots those values.

Step 2 — `setPhone(newPhone)` changes only the phone field in memory.

Step 3 — at flush, dirty checking compares against the snapshot and finds only phone changed. Because the entity has `@DynamicUpdate`, Hibernate generates `update accounts set phone=? where id=?`, touching no other column, so the balance trigger does not fire.

Step 4 — commit makes the change permanent; name and balance are untouched.

Step 5 (broken path contrast) — building `new Account(id)` and setting only phone leaves name and balance null; `merge` copies all of that detached state onto the managed row, so name and balance are written as null, wiping the stored values.

```
2026-10-24 01:17:02 INFO  Phone updated for SAV2001; only the phone column will be written
2026-10-24 01:17:02 DEBUG Hibernate: update accounts set phone=? where id=?
2026-10-24 01:17:05 WARN  Merged a partial entity — name and balance may be wiped!
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  PATCH /accounts/SAV2001/phone {"phone":"987..."}
    │
    ├─ CORRECT (load + mutate)            ├─ BROKEN (merge partial)
    │  find(id) → full managed            │  new Account(id); setPhone()
    │   name=Rajesh balance=1,000,000     │   name=null balance=null
    │  setPhone("987...")                 │  merge(partial)
    │  dirty check → phone only           │  copies ALL state incl. nulls
    │  @DynamicUpdate                     │  UPDATE sets name=NULL, balance=NULL
    ▼                                     ▼
  UPDATE accounts SET phone=? WHERE id=? UPDATE blanks name & balance
  name/balance preserved               stored data WIPED
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Dirty Check, @DynamicUpdate, merge pitfall (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Unit of Work + dirty checking (snapshot comparison)       │
  │  Partial-update via load-and-mutate (avoids merge nulls)   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: service updates; entity owns its state                 │
  │  L: partial updates don't violate entity invariants        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Mechanism (as prose) ──
  Default UPDATE: static, all columns, reusable prepared statement.
  @DynamicUpdate: runtime SQL, only dirty columns, small per-flush cost.
  merge(detached): copies ENTIRE detached state → null fields overwrite.

  ── State Diagram: an update ──
  [MANAGED+snapshot] ─setField─▶ [DIRTY] ─flush─▶ compare snapshot
        │ @DynamicUpdate → changed cols only
        │ default        → all cols
        ▼
  [UPDATE executed]

  ── Call Chain (correct) ──
  1. find(id) → managed (full state)
  2. setPhone(x) → dirty on phone
  3. flush → @DynamicUpdate → UPDATE phone only
  4. commit (name/balance untouched)

  (Caution) merge(partial DTO-entity) → null-overwrite. (Caution) @DynamicUpdate still honors @Version.
  Rule: partial update = load the entity and mutate; never merge a half-built object.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
By default Hibernate generates one static update statement per entity that lists every mapped column, so even when I change a single field the SQL writes all of them. This is intentional: preparing one statement once and reusing it is cheaper than building a custom statement on every flush, and it cooperates well with the JDBC statement cache. The decision of whether to update at all comes from dirty checking, where Hibernate snapshots the entity's fields when it becomes managed and, at flush, compares the current values to that snapshot; if anything differs the entity is dirty and the update runs.

The all-columns behavior is usually harmless, but it causes problems on wide tables, on tables with triggers, or where unnecessary writes matter, because it writes columns that did not change and can fire database triggers or audit logic you did not intend. Putting the annotation for dynamic update on the entity tells Hibernate to generate the update at runtime with only the dirty columns, so a phone change produces an update that sets only the phone. I apply it selectively, because generating SQL per flush has a small cost and loses the reusable prepared statement.

The separate and more dangerous issue is the merge null-overwrite trap. The merge operation copies the entire state of a detached entity onto the managed entity loaded from the database, so if I build an entity from an incoming request that only set the phone and left the name and balance null, merge copies those nulls over the stored values and wipes them. At National Bank of India a profile update API did exactly this and blanked customers' names. The fix, which is also my standard pattern, is to load the managed entity by id and set only the fields I actually intend to change, letting dirty checking persist the partial update, rather than merging a half-built object. The nuances I always mention are that dynamic update still honors the optimistic lock version column, and that for partial updates I prefer load-and-mutate or an explicit update query over mapping a request DTO straight onto an entity and merging it.

---

keyPoints: Default: UPDATE all columns even if only one changed
Wastes bandwidth, increases DB write amplification
Fix: @DynamicUpdate on entity — only changed columns in SET clause
Trade-off: Hibernate must compare old vs new values — slight CPU overhead
